title: From a Week to a Month
sub: Grades 1–2 · Carter G. Woodson and Black History Month
objective: Children will learn that Black History Month began as a single week. In 1926 the historian Carter G. Woodson started Negro History Week so that schoolchildren would learn Black history, and he chose February for the birthdays of Abraham Lincoln and Frederick Douglass. The week later became a month. Children will count a week into a month, hear the names the poster honors, and think about how museums keep history safe.

objectives.heading: By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
objectives.why: Carter G. Woodson wanted every schoolchild to learn Black history. Every February, when we learn it, we do what he hoped.

materials: Poster 1, *Black History Month*: page 3 of this plan, projected or printed, or the poster in the exhibition
A wall calendar, open at February
Differentiated handouts, one per child; crayons
questions: What is a historian? What would you like to study about the past?
Why did Carter G. Woodson want schoolchildren to learn Black history?
Why is Black History Month in February?
If you could keep one story, place or object safe for people in the future, what would it be, and why?
connection: **Visit the exhibition:** stand in front of poster 1 and find the musician, the singer, the worker and the scientist in its ring. **Online,** the poster’s walkthrough reads each paragraph aloud.

steps.title: What do you see?
script: Show poster 1 and say nothing yet. Ask: *“Look at the circles. Who do you see? What are they doing?”* Children may find a musician, a singer at a microphone, a worker in a cap, a scientist at a microscope, music notes and an atom. Then point to the big words: *“This says Black History Month. Every February, we learn about Black history. But it did not start as a month. It started as one week.”*

screen.alt: Poster 1, Black History Month, on an acid lime ground: a ring of circular illustrated vignettes — a musician, a singer at a microphone, a worker in a cap and a scientist at a microscope, music notes and an atom — around a black shape lettered Black History Month, above three paragraphs of text
screen.caption: Poster 1 · *Black History Month*

steps.purpose: Look at the poster’s pictures before any words: who is in them, and what are they doing?
students: Look at the circles. Who do you see?

steps.title: A historian
script: Tell the story: *“A long time ago there was a man called Carter G. Woodson. He was a **historian**, a person who studies the past. He believed Black history should not stay with scholars in universities. He wanted everyone to learn it. So in 1926 he started a special week to teach schoolchildren Black history. He called it Negro History Week.”* (*Negro* is an old word people used then for Black Americans. Today we say Black or African American.)

screen.text:
Carter G. Woodson
A historian
1926: Negro History Week

steps.purpose: Meet Carter G. Woodson, the historian who wanted schoolchildren to learn Black history.

steps.title: Why February?
script: Ask: *“Why do you think Woodson chose February?”* Take guesses. Then: *“He chose February because two famous Americans had their birthdays in February: Abraham Lincoln and Frederick Douglass.”* Find February on the calendar.

screen.question: Why do you think Woodson chose February?

steps.purpose: Wonder first, then hear the poster’s answer: two birthdays.

steps.title: A week grew into a month
script: *“Woodson’s week later became Black History Month.”* Count seven days on the calendar for one week, then show the whole month. *“One week grew into a whole month!”*

screen.text:
1926: one week
Today: a whole month

steps.purpose: See the week grow: seven days became a month.
students: How many days are in a week?
Is a month longer or shorter?

steps.title: People we honor
script: Read the three names the poster honors: Martin Luther King Jr., Harriet Tubman and Langston Hughes. Ask who has heard of them, and what the children would like to find out. Write their questions down to explore later in the month.

screen.text:
Martin Luther King Jr.
Harriet Tubman
Langston Hughes

steps.purpose: Hear three names the poster honors, and wonder what we would like to find out.
students: What would you like to find out?

steps.title: History keepers
script: The poster says that museums help keep Black history safe: people give **artifacts**, special objects, to museums so that everyone can remember. Ask: *“What would you give to a museum, so people remember?”* Children tell a partner about something special from their family: a photograph, a recipe, a song.

screen.question: What would you give to a museum, so people remember?

steps.purpose: Connect the poster’s idea of preserving history to the children’s own lives.
students: Think of something special from your family.

steps.title: Choose a handout
script: Then children choose a handout; all three levels find February and count a week.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Circle February, color seven boxes for a week, draw something to give a museum, and trace the word *history*.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Circle February, finish the story with a word bank, count the days in four weeks, and draw and label something to keep safe.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Write why Woodson chose February and why he wanted children to learn Black history, write a question about a person the poster honors, and design a circle picture like the poster’s.

steps.purpose: Practice the story on paper, at the right level of challenge.
students: Choose Green, Yellow or Red. All three find February, count a week, and keep history safe.

steps.section: Look back and pass it on
steps.title: Look back
script: Put the questions on the screen. For each one, children show a thumb up, sideways or down: *“Can you now say who Carter G. Woodson was, and what he started? Can you tell why Black History Month is in February? Can you show how a week grew into a month? Can you say how museums keep history safe?”*

steps.title: Pass it on
script: Then say: *“Woodson wanted every child to learn Black history. Tell a partner one thing you learned today. Now you are passing it on!”*
